label: Yehezkel (Ezekiel) — Part 1 — Chapters 1–11
summary_plain: Yehezkel sees the heavens opened by the river Kevar in Babylon. He sees four living creatures with four faces — man, lion, ox, eagle — and wheels within wheels full of eyes. Above them is a throne of sapphire, and on the throne a figure like the appearance of a man surrounded by fire and radiance. YHWH sends Yehezkel to speak to the rebellious house. He eats a scroll. He lies on his side for 390 days. He sees the elders of Yisra'EL worshipping abominations in the Temple — including women weeping for Tammuz at the north gate.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from the DSS Ezekiel fragments (4QEzek-a, 4QEzek-b, 4QEzek-c, 11QEzek) and the Orit Ge'ez. The throne vision (Merkavah) in chapter 1 is the most elaborate divine throne description in the covenant literature — more detailed than Yesha'yahu 6 or Chanokh 14. Chapter 8:14 documents women weeping for Tammuz at the north gate of the Temple — the Babylonian dying-rising deity whose mourning cycle structurally parallels the Easter death-resurrection tradition.

key_terms.definition: The divine chariot-throne in Yehezkel 1; YHWH's mobile throne borne by four living creatures with wheels; this vision launched one of the most significant traditions in Jewish mysticism — merkavah mysticism.

The four living beings in Yehezkel 1: each has four faces (human, lion, ox, eagle), four wings, and straight legs; they carry YHWH's chariot-throne; they form the foundation of the heavenly transport.

The interlocked wheels in Yehezkel 1:15-21 that go in any direction without turning; they are full of eyes all around and are the chariot's mobility system; 'the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.'

An untranslatable Hebrew word in Yehezkel 1:4,27 — describing the gleaming substance or luminous fire around YHWH's form on the chariot-throne; associated with brilliance and electrum or polished bronze.

YHWH addresses Yehezkel as 'Ben Adam' (son of man/human) throughout the book; at his call, Yehezkel is given a scroll with lamentations and woe written on it, which he eats and finds as sweet as honey.

YHWH addresses Yehezkel as 'ben adam' (son of man/human) over 90 times in the book — an emphatic contrast between the human prophet and the divine glory he stands before; the term underscores Yehezkel's creaturely status before YHWH.

YHWH commands Yehezkel to perform elaborate enacted prophecies: lying on his left side 390 days (Yisra'el's punishment) and right side 40 days (Yehudah's), cooking bread over dung, shaving his head and dividing the hair to signify Yerushalayim's fate.

Yehezkel was commanded to lie on his left side 390 days bearing the iniquity of the house of Yisra'el (one day per year of punishment) and on his right side 40 days for the house of Yehudah — a prolonged embodied prophecy of the exile's duration.

In a devastating vision, Yehezkel watches YHWH's glory (kavod YHWH) leave the Temple in stages: from the inner sanctuary to the threshold (10:4), then to the east gate (10:19), then to the Mount of Olives (11:23) — YHWH withdrawing his presence from the doomed Temple.
The river or canal in Babylonia where Yehezkel received his initial visions among the Babylonian exile community; 'by the Chebar canal' opens the first chapter and several subsequent visions.

faq.question: What is the Merkavah vision in Yehezkel 1?
faq.answer: The Merkavah (chariot-throne) vision in Yehezkel 1 is the most elaborate divine-throne vision in the Hebrew corpus. YHWH's glory appears on a mobile chariot-throne borne by four living creatures (Khayot) with four faces, four wings, and wheels-within-wheels. The vision was given in Babylonia — demonstrating that YHWH's presence is not confined to the Temple or the land of Yehudah.

faq.question: Why is Yehezkel called 'Ben Adam' (son of man) throughout the book?
faq.answer: YHWH addresses Yehezkel as 'ben adam' — literally 'son of man/human' — over 90 times. This is not a title but an emphatic contrast: in the presence of overwhelming divine glory, Yehezkel is continually reminded of his creaturely, human status. It is the same phrase used in Tehillim 8:4 ('what is a human being that you are mindful of him?') — the creature before the Creator.

faq.question: What did the scroll that Yehezkel ate represent?
faq.answer: In Yehezkel 2:8-3:3, YHWH gives Yehezkel a scroll written with lamentations, mourning, and woe, and commands him to eat it. The scroll represents YHWH's word of judgment; eating it means fully internalizing that word before speaking it. The paradox: it is bitter content (lamentation and woe) but it tastes sweet as honey — YHWH's word is always good, even when its content is judgment.

faq.question: What is the theological significance of YHWH's glory departing the Temple in Yehezkel 10-11?
faq.answer: The departure of YHWH's glory from the Temple is the most devastating event in Yehezkel's entire vision: YHWH is withdrawing his protecting presence before the Babylonians arrive. The departure is in stages — giving time for the vision to be fully grasped. The city is not destroyed by an invasion alone; YHWH leaves before the walls fall. His presence, not the building, was the city's true protection.

faq.question: What is Yehezkel 11:19-20's 'heart of stone / heart of flesh' promise?
faq.answer: YHWH promises to give the exiles one heart and a new spirit, removing the heart of stone (stubbornness, inability to respond to YHWH) and replacing it with a heart of flesh (responsive, capable of covenant faithfulness). This anticipates Yirmeyahu 31's new covenant with Torah written on the heart — both texts describe the same transformation of covenant capacity.

faq.question: Why did YHWH command Yehezkel to perform sign-acts rather than simply speak prophecy?
faq.answer: Sign-acts in Yehezkel communicate through embodied reality: 390 days lying on his side, 40 days, cooking bread over dung, dividing shaved hair into thirds. These enacted prophecies make the word visible and experiential — the prophet's body becomes the message. For an audience that dismissed the spoken word, the prolonged, public, physical acts could not be ignored or explained away.

faq.question: What are the Ophanim (wheels) in Yehezkel 1?
faq.answer: The Ophanim are the wheels of YHWH's chariot-throne. Each wheel is described as a 'wheel within a wheel' — an interlocking design that allows movement in any of four directions without turning. Their rims are full of eyes, and the spirit of the living creatures is in the wheels — the wheels move wherever the creatures go, as one unified divine transport system.

faq.question: What is the significance of the mark on the foreheads in Yehezkel 9?
faq.answer: In Yehezkel 9, before the slaughter of Yerushalayim's inhabitants begins, YHWH commands a heavenly scribe to put a mark (tav — the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet) on the foreheads of those who sighed and groaned over the abominations. These are spared; everyone else is killed. The mark identifies those who maintained moral grief in the midst of systemic idolatry — a covenant remnant within the condemned city.

faq.question: Why does the Merkavah vision appear in Babylonia rather than in Yerushalayim?
faq.answer: The vision appearing in Babylonia — not in the Temple — is itself a theological statement: YHWH is not confined to his Temple. He can appear on a mobile chariot-throne beside the Chebar canal in Chaldea. This was essential comfort and commission for the exiles: YHWH did not abandon them when they were exiled; he went with them, mobile throne and all.

faq.question: What abominations does Yehezkel 8 describe in the Temple?
faq.answer: In a transported vision of Yerushalayim, Yehezkel 8 shows four escalating abominations in the Temple: (1) the idol of jealousy at the north gate; (2) seventy elders burning incense to animal-images in a hidden room; (3) women weeping for Tammuz at the Temple gate; (4) twenty-five men with their backs to the Temple bowing east to the sun. Each abomination is worse than the last — total syncretistic corruption.

faq.question: What does Yehezkel 3:17 mean when YHWH calls Yehezkel a watchman?
faq.answer: YHWH appoints Yehezkel as a watchman (tzofeh) for the house of Yisra'el. If the watchman does not warn when the sword comes, the people die in their iniquity but their blood is on the watchman. If Yehezkel warns and they do not listen, they die in their iniquity but Yehezkel is cleared. The watchman metaphor defines prophetic accountability: the obligation is to deliver the warning, not to control the response.
